content: The Care for Infants and Young Children Implementation Review and Planning Guide is a comprehensive document designed to improve the quality of primary health care services for infants and young children. It is part of the Primary Health Care Quality Improvement Guide series, specifically Module 3, which focuses on the care of infants and children. This guide is published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2024 and is available under a Creative Commons license, allowing for non-commercial use, adaptation, and redistribution, provided proper citation is given. The guide emphasizes that any use of the material should not imply endorsement by WHO of specific organizations, products, or services. The WHO logo cannot be used in association with the material. If the guide is adapted, the resulting work must be licensed under the same or an equivalent Creative Commons license. Translations of the guide must include a disclaimer stating that the translation was not created by WHO and that the original English version remains the authoritative edition. The guide is part of a series of modules aimed at improving primary health care quality. These include: 1. Preventing unplanned pregnancies through outpatient family planning services. 2. Antenatal care services. 3. Care for infants and young children. The focus of Module 3 is on children from birth to three years of age, who are at the highest risk of morbidity and mortality. It outlines survive interventions, which address illnesses responsible for most child deaths, such as vaccination, Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI), and nutrition for infants and young children. It also includes thrive interventions, which promote early childhood development and prevent disabilities, injuries, violence, abuse, and neglect. Programs must ensure the effective delivery of both survive and thrive interventions. As coverage of survive interventions increases and child mortality declines, thrive interventions are typically added. The guide is intended for use in primary-care facilities, such as health centers, health posts, and outpatient departments of hospitals. While it covers pre-referral care, advanced management of cases is beyond its scope. Programs not administered through health facilities, such as iodized salt distribution, are also excluded. The guide provides tools for continuous monitoring and periodic evaluations of child health services. It includes checklists to assess the quality of clinical care, policies, supplies, and environments. These checklists help identify areas needing improvement and actions to address them. For periodic evaluations, external teams use the same checklists to assess services across multiple facilities and develop plans based on the data. The guide also outlines a process for continuous monitoring of child health services at primary-care clinics. A team of facility staff, paired with a trained external facilitator, conducts assessments and develops a three-month quality improvement plan. Internal self-assessments are repeated to track progress. The recommended participants include two to four facility staff, including the facility manager and clinical care providers. In larger hospitals, quality-assurance staff may also be involved. The process typically requires one day for facility review and action plan development. The guide includes a table of core survive-and-thrive interventions for infants and young children, covering areas such as feeding, nutrition, vaccination, prevention and management of common childhood illnesses, HIV and tuberculosis, injuries, and early childhood development. It also provides key steps for child health planning reviews at primary-care clinics, including hospitals, health centers, and health posts. The WHO emphasizes the importance of ensuring healthy growth and development for all children, as they represent the future. Despite significant progress in reducing child mortality rates, challenges remain, particularly for poor, rural, and less-educated populations. The guide aims to address these challenges by improving the quality of primary health care services for children, engaging local staff in problem-solving, and tracking progress through data collection and monitoring.
